passage: In their Nairobi flat, Wanjiru, who was five, finished her sweet and held out her hand for another. "No more today," Mama said, putting the tin on the high shelf. Wanjiru's face went hot. Her friend Selin, visiting, still had half of hers. "It's not fair!" Wanjiru stamped both feet so hard the cups rattled. "I hate you!" she shouted, then burst into tears and stamped again.

qa.q: Where did Mama put the tin?
qa.a: On the high shelf.

qa.q: What was Wanjiru feeling when she shouted 'I hate you'?
qa.a: She felt angry and that it was unfair, especially with Selin still eating, and her body reacted before her words could.

qa.q: What could Mama say next that keeps the limit?
qa.a: Something calm like, 'You're really angry. The answer is still no more today,' without shouting back or giving in.

qa.q: How might Selin feel watching this?
qa.a: Selin may feel awkward or a little scared, holding her half-eaten sweet while Wanjiru stamps and cries.

grounding: Shows a five-year-old refused a second sweet feeling it is unfair, her body reacting with stamping and 'I hate you' before words.

passage: Teacher's note, Nursery B, Monday. At tidy-up, Deepika wanted more time with the clay. First she cried. When I said, "Tidy-up time now," she tried promising: "Just two minutes, I'll tidy everything, I promise!" Then she watched my face very carefully. When I said no again, she shouted, "You're mean!" and looked to see what I would do. Last week a helper gave in to her, and I think she remembers. Today I kept the same calm words and helped her put the clay away. Irfan, beside her, watched the whole thing. Tomorrow I'll give a five-minute warning before tidy-up.

qa.q: What did Deepika want more time with?
qa.a: She wanted more time with the clay.

qa.q: Why did Deepika watch the teacher's face so carefully?
qa.a: She was testing, hopeful that promising or shouting might move the limit, as it had when a helper gave in last week.

qa.q: Why does keeping the same calm answer matter now?
qa.a: If the limit moves after crying or shouting, Deepika learns that tantrums work; staying calm and consistent teaches her they don't.

qa.q: What might Irfan be learning as he watches?
qa.a: Irfan may feel curious and a bit unsettled, and he also sees that shouting did not change the rule.

grounding: Shows a young child cycling through crying, promising and shouting while watching to see whether the limit will move.

passage: The power had gone out at seven, the fan was dead, and Vikas had just walked in from a ten-hour shift. Zubin, five, wanted to play on the phone. "Not now, beta. The battery's low." Zubin threw his car across the floor. "I hate you! You're the worst papa!" Vikas felt the words land like a slap. Heat rushed up his neck. He wanted to roar, "Go to your room!" louder than Zubin. His finger was already pointing. Then he noticed it: the tight jaw, the pointing finger. He dropped his hand and breathed out slowly, once, twice, in the dark, hot room.

qa.q: How long was the shift Vikas had just finished?
qa.a: It was a ten-hour shift.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when Zubin shouted 'I hate you'?
qa.a: He felt stung and angry, heat rushing up his neck, and was tempted to roar back louder than Zubin.

qa.q: What was the key moment in this scene, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Vikas noticed his tight jaw and pointing finger and breathed before acting, which gives him the chance to respond calmly instead of matching Zubin's volume.

qa.q: What might Zubin be feeling when he throws his car?
qa.a: Zubin is frustrated and angry at being refused, and 'I hate you' is that big feeling spilling out, not a true measure of his love.

grounding: Shows a tired parent stung by a child's 'I hate you', tempted to shout or punish, pausing to notice his own heat and breathe first.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, a jar of toffees sat on the reception desk. Simran, five, had already had one from Baljeet at the counter. "Another! Papa, another!" Sumit shook his head. Simran's voice rose. "I hate you! Give it!" People looked up. Sumit crouched to her eye level and spoke low and steady. "I hear you're angry. The answer is still no more sweets today." He didn't bargain, didn't scold, didn't call her naughty. Simran howled and pushed his arm. He stayed, calm, arms open. "I'm right here when you want a hug."

qa.q: Who gave Simran her first toffee?
qa.a: Baljeet at the counter.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when she pushed Sumit's arm?
qa.a: She was angry and frustrated that the limit held, her big feelings still spilling over.

qa.q: Which parts of Sumit's response make the limit calm and firm?
qa.a: He crouched to her level, named her anger, repeated the no without bargaining, shaming or shouting, and stayed ready to hug.

qa.q: How might the people in the waiting room see Sumit?
qa.a: They may be surprised to see a parent stay so steady, and perhaps relieved there is no shouting match.

grounding: Shows a parent naming a child's anger while holding a firm no on sweets, without shaming, bargaining or shouting, and staying open for comfort.

passage: At the community centre playgroup, Sabina had cried and shouted for ten minutes because her painted kite had to stay until it dried. Now she was quiet, hiccupping. Abbu, who had come to fetch her, sat on the low bench. Sabina edged closer, peeking at him, then climbed into his lap and hid her face in his shirt. "I said you're a bad Abbu," she whispered. "Am I still your Sabina?" Abbu held her close. "Always. Even when you're angry." Sabina's shoulders dropped. Jahnavi Ma'am, packing away paints, smiled. "The kite will be dry tomorrow, Sabina."

qa.q: Why did Sabina's painted kite have to stay at the playgroup?
qa.a: It had to stay until it dried.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel as she hid her face in Abbu's shirt?
qa.a: She felt ashamed of calling him a bad Abbu and relieved to be held, needing to know she was still loved.

qa.q: Why was Abbu's answer the right one at this stage?
qa.a: By saying 'Always. Even when you're angry', he showed her that her anger had not broken their bond.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi Ma'am feel watching them?
qa.a: Jahnavi Ma'am seems warm and pleased to see Sabina comforted, and adds a reassuring word about the kite.

grounding: Shows a child after a tantrum climbing into her father's lap, ashamed and relieved, needing to know she is still loved.

passage: Note for Pooja's teacher, from her mother, Ganga. You asked how the angry mornings were going. Last night Pooja and I made an angry list together. She drew three pictures: feet stomping softly, a crayon scribbling hard on scrap paper, and two arms for "ask for a hug". I also told her, "This morning I raised my voice. I'm sorry. I'll try the list too." She looked surprised, then patted my cheek. Today, when her sock felt wrong, she stomped softly across the room, giggled and asked for a hug. The list is on our fridge. Could you try it at school?

qa.q: What three pictures did Pooja draw?
qa.a: Feet stomping softly, a crayon scribbling hard on scrap paper, and two arms for "ask for a hug".

qa.q: What did Pooja's pat on her mother's cheek suggest she felt?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and touched by the apology, and forgiving, glad her mother could say sorry too.

qa.q: Why is Ganga's apology part of the skill-building?
qa.a: By owning her raised voice, she shows Pooja that everyone can make things right, not only children.

qa.q: What might Pooja's teacher think on reading the note?
qa.a: The teacher may feel encouraged and ready to try the angry list at school so Pooja has the same tools there.

grounding: Shows a parent and child later planning what to do when angry, and the parent apologising for a raised voice, modelling repair.

passage: I've taught science at this school for eleven years, and I almost missed Rekha. She sat in the third row, never raised her hand and wrote very small. But in March she waited after class until the others had gone and asked, "Ma'am, if light slows down in water, where does the extra energy go?" Nobody had asked me that in years. The next week she asked why onions make us cry, and whether it was the same kind of chemistry. Her questions were careful, as if she had turned them over for days. So I lent her an old popular-science book from my shelf and said, "Only if you're interested." She held it in both hands as if it might break. A week later she returned it with fourteen small paper slips marking pages. I'm Neelam, and I still keep that book.

qa.q: How many paper slips were in the book when Rekha returned it?
qa.a: Fourteen small paper slips marking pages.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel when Rekha asked about light slowing down in water?
qa.a: Neelam felt surprised and delighted, since nobody had asked such a careful question in years.

qa.q: What did Neelam do that made the most of this moment?
qa.a: She lent the book gently, 'only if you're interested', giving Rekha room to say yes without pressure.

qa.q: What might it have felt like for Rekha to be handed that book?
qa.a: Rekha probably felt surprised and quietly proud to be noticed by a teacher, holding the book carefully as if it might break.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a quiet student's careful questions and offering extra reading, and how being noticed moves the student.

passage: Teacher's notebook, Afreen Ma'am, Biology, Thursday. Hafsa came to my desk after school again, the third time this month. She hovers first, pretending to read the notice board. Today she finally said, "Ma'am, can I ask something stupid?" I said there was no such thing. She asked whether it was wrong to want to be a doctor if she feels faint at the sight of blood. She watched my face closely, as if waiting for me to laugh. I didn't. I told her it was a real question, and that some doctors work in labs or research and rarely see blood. Her shoulders came down. Then she told me more: her family expects medicine, and she isn't sure she wants it at all. We will meet again next week, and I'll bring information on other paths too.

qa.q: What did Hafsa ask before her real question?
qa.a: She asked, "Ma'am, can I ask something stupid?"

qa.q: Why did Hafsa watch Afreen Ma'am's face so closely?
qa.a: She was nervous and unsure, testing whether the teacher would take her seriously or laugh at her worry about blood.

qa.q: What made Hafsa open up further?
qa.a: Afreen Ma'am treated the question as real and answered respectfully, which lowered Hafsa's guard enough to share her family's expectations.

qa.q: How might Hafsa's family see her doubts?
qa.a: Her family expects medicine, so they may be surprised or worried to learn she isn't sure she wants it.

grounding: Shows a student cautiously bringing doubts about becoming a doctor to a teacher, testing the reaction, and relaxing with each respectful reply.

passage: Uday, you think your Avni Dadi always had her own opinions? At fifteen I worshipped Mr Bose, our physics teacher. He said "Elementary!" whenever something was obvious, so I said "Elementary!" at dinner until my brothers begged me to stop. He thought poetry was a waste of time, so I stopped reading poetry, though I had loved it since I was small. If he said a film was foolish, it was foolish. My notebooks were full of his phrases. That admiration made me study harder than ever, it's true. But one day he wrote a wrong answer on the board, and I defended it to my friend Kamala for twenty minutes before I checked the book. My own head had gone quiet, beta. I had handed it over to him.

qa.q: What did Mr Bose say whenever something was obvious?
qa.a: He said "Elementary!"

qa.q: How did the young Avni feel about Mr Bose?
qa.a: She felt a deep, eager admiration, almost worship, so strong that she echoed his phrases and gave up the poetry she loved.

qa.q: When the young Avni checked the book and found Mr Bose's answer was wrong, what could she take from that turning point?
qa.a: She could keep admiring him while using her own judgement again, checking facts herself and returning to the poetry she loved.

qa.q: What might Kamala have felt during those twenty minutes of argument?
qa.a: Kamala may have felt frustrated and puzzled that her friend defended a wrong answer so fiercely just because Mr Bose had said it.

grounding: Shows a student idealising a teacher, copying his phrases and taking his opinions as truth, which fuels effort but hides his limits and her own judgement.

passage:
Tuesday. Rukmini Ma'am handed back Uma's project on river pollution with red ink all over the second half. "Your data is strong, but your conclusion ignores half of it. You can do much better than this." Uma's face burned. She had stayed up till midnight. She stuffed the file into her bag without a word.
Wednesday. Uma told her friend, "She hates me now." Then she reread the comments at night. Annoyingly, they were right. At the bottom, in small letters, Ma'am had written: "I push because you can go far."
The following Monday. Uma brought a new draft. Rukmini Ma'am read it slowly, then smiled. "Now this is your real work." Uma walked out feeling taller, and slightly embarrassed about Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Uma's project about?
qa.a: Her project was on river pollution.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she stuffed the file into her bag?
qa.a: She felt stung and angry, her face burning after staying up till midnight on it.

qa.q: What helped Uma turn the criticism into better work?
qa.a: Rereading the comments calmly and seeing they were right, helped by the note showing the teacher pushed her because she could go far.

qa.q: What might Rukmini Ma'am be feeling as she writes the red comments?
qa.a: She probably cares and has high hopes for Uma, even knowing the bluntness will sting, as her note 'you can go far' shows.

grounding: Shows a teacher bluntly critiquing a student's project with warmth underneath, and the student moving from stung anger to seeing the criticism as a gift.
